name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Standardize a shared glossary of terms across all departments. Marketing, product, and creative teams all use the same words differently—"campaign," "asset," "release," "version"—which causes misaligned priorities and duplicated work. One person from each department drafts a 10-term list in a week, then we lock it in a single doc. The trade-off is slower initial setup for faster execution later.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The glossary won’t stop the bleeding. If Marketing calls a "campaign" a 3-month push and Product calls it a 2-week sprint, a shared list of words won’t fix the conflict—it just gives them a dictionary to argue over. Instead, force the three departments to co-write a single "campaign charter" that defines what a campaign is, who owns it, and when it’s "done." That artifact forces trade-offs; the glossary just polishes the knife.

name: Chisel
text:
Run a one-page "campaign charter" template that Marketing, Product, and Creative co-write in a 90-minute live session. It forces them to agree on one definition of "campaign," one start/end date, and one success metric up front. The trade-off is that the charter will feel rigid at first, but it stops the bigger waste of rework and misaligned priorities.
[dispatched 4 workers: worker-7756, worker-2082, worker-5278… — done, dissolved]

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s 90-minute charter risks forcing a false consensus—teams will nod to move on, not to align. Instead, require each department to submit their *minimum* definition of "campaign" up front, then run a 30-minute mediation to surface the real conflict. The artifact is the *disagreement log*, not the charter; that log is the only thing that forces honest trade-offs.

name: Scope
text: Run a one-page "campaign charter" template co-written live by Marketing, Product, and Creative in a 90-minute session. It forces them to agree on one definition of "campaign," one start/end date, and one success metric up front. The trade-off is rigidity at first, but it stops the bleeding of misaligned priorities and duplicated work.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The 90-minute charter forces premature agreement—teams will trade real clarity for speed. Instead, require each department to submit their *minimum* definition of "campaign" up front, then run a 30-minute mediation to surface the real conflict. The artifact is the *disagreement log*, not the charter.

name: Reel
text: Run a 30-minute mediation session where each department submits their *minimum* definition of "campaign" up front, then surfaces the real conflict. The artifact is the *disagreement log*—not a forced consensus. This avoids false agreement and exposes the real trade-offs early. The trade-off is that it delays the start of work, but it prevents wasted effort on misaligned priorities.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The 30-minute mediation risks boiling the conflict down to a single log entry—teams will oversimplify to fit the timebox, not to resolve the core misalignment. Instead, require each department to submit their *minimum* definition in writing 48 hours before the session, then run a 60-minute structured debate with a neutral facilitator. The artifact is the *decision record*: one agreed definition, one start/end date, and one success metric—signed by all three leads. That forces real trade-offs, not just a log of them.

name: Chisel
text: Run a 48-hour written pre-work phase where Marketing, Product, and Creative each submit their *minimum* definition of "campaign" in one paragraph, then convene a 60-minute live mediation to compare the three documents side-by-side. The artifact is the *disagreement log* with three columns—one per department—so the conflict is visible, not buried. This forces clarity before the meeting and prevents false consensus or oversimplification. The trade-off is the 48-hour delay, but it’s the only way to surface real misalignment early.

name: Sift
text: The 48-hour written pre-work risks teams gaming the system—marketing writes a vague paragraph to avoid locking in dates, product over-constrains scope to hit a metric, and creative hides ambiguity in "brand tone." Instead, require each department to submit a *single sentence* definition of "campaign" and a *single data point* they’ll track—no paragraphs, no wiggle room. The artifact is the three sentences side-by-side; if they can’t agree on the words, the conflict isn’t hidden, it’s exposed.

name: Chisel
text: Run a 60-minute mediation session where Marketing, Product, and Creative each submit their *minimum* definition of "campaign" in writing 48 hours before the meeting. The lead facilitator (Marketing) surfaces the real conflicts in a shared disagreement log during the session. This forces clarity without forcing false consensus up front. The trade-off is slower initial alignment, but it prevents costly misalignment later.

name: Sift
text: The 60-minute mediation with pre-submitted definitions risks teams gaming the system—submitting vague, high-level definitions to avoid conflict, then using the session to argue over interpretations rather than trade-offs. Instead, require each department to submit *one concrete example* of a past campaign they consider successful, then run a 45-minute session to compare them side-by-side. The artifact is the *example comparison table*—not a log. This exposes real misalignment faster than abstract definitions.

name: Scope
text: Run a 48-hour pre-work sprint where each department submits one concrete past campaign example that best represents their view of "campaign." The lead facilitator (Marketing) compiles these into a shared artifact by hour 48. This forces specificity over vagueness—no one can hide behind buzzwords when forced to pick a real example. The trade-off is slower initial output, but it guarantees the disagreement log starts with real stakes, not recycled definitions.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The 48-hour pre-work sprint risks departments cherry-picking examples that fit their narrative, not the real conflict. Instead, require each department to submit *one* past campaign that *failed* for them—this exposes where their definition broke down. The artifact is the *failure log*, and the lead (Marketing) compiles it by hour 48; if the examples align, the conflict is artificial—if not, the trade-offs are real.
